planting.note: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost date, then transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Start seeds indoors in peat pots 3 to 4 weeks before your last frost date, or direct sow once soil has warmed past 70°F, then thin or space plants generously to allow the sprawling vines room to run. Released by Cornell plant breeder Henry Munger in 1944 as a cross of 'Minnesota 99-36' and 'Bender's Surprise', Iroquois was the first muskmelon bred specifically for resistance to Fusarium wilt. Its thick, heavily netted rind covers deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, musky-sweet flavor, and its disease tolerance made it a long-time favorite for northern and Midwestern home gardens.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

common_name: Pride of Wisconsin Melon (Queen of Colorado Muskmelon)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost date, then transplant out once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.

directions: Start seeds indoors a few weeks ahead of the last frost to give this melon a head start in shorter growing seasons, then transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. Originally sold as 'Queen of Colorado' in the early 1920s before being reintroduced under its current name in 1937, this heirloom produces oval, 4 to 8 pound melons with apricot-orange flesh that is notably sweet with little of the musky aftertaste typical of many muskmelons. It was long grown as a market melon for Milwaukee before nearly disappearing from trade, and it remains valued today for good powdery mildew tolerance.

common_name: Eden's Gem Melon (Rocky Ford Green-Flesh Muskmelon)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed and all danger of frost has passed, in hills spaced to give vines room to spread.

directions: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed, spacing hills to let the compact vines spread, and water evenly while fruit is sizing. Developed at Rocky Ford, Colorado and introduced in 1905 as a descendant of the older Green Nutmeg melon, Eden's Gem produces softball-sized, heavily netted fruit with green flesh and a distinctive spicy-sweet flavor. Its early maturity made it a popular shipping melon in the early twentieth century, and it remains prized by heirloom growers for its complex flavor in a compact package.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost, giving vines plenty of room to sprawl in full sun.

directions: Sow directly into warm soil once frost danger has passed, and provide consistent moisture while vines establish and fruit sizes up. This heirloom traces to the Melitopol region of southern Ukraine, a historic melon and watermelon growing district, and was bred for a relatively short, reliable season compared to many large Southern watermelon types. Fruits are round with dark green striping and crisp, sweet pink-red flesh, making it a favorite among gardeners in cooler climates who still want an authentic watermelon harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost, or transplant young seedlings for an earlier start in short-season areas.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed, or start transplants a few weeks early to get a jump on the season, and thin to strong single plants once vines begin to run. New Queen was named an All-America Selections winner in 1999 for its early, compact icebox-sized fruit and its unusual bright orange-yellow flesh, a departure from typical red-fleshed watermelons of its era. The globe-shaped fruits typically weigh 5 to 6 pounds and offer crisp, honey-sweet flavor well suited to small gardens.

common_name: Cream of the Crop Acorn Squash (White Bush Acorn Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed, once soil has warmed thoroughly.

directions: Direct sow into warm soil once frost risk has passed, spacing plants for their compact bush habit which suits smaller garden beds. Cream of the Crop was named an All-America Selections winner in 1990 for its productive bush vines and creamy white-skinned acorn-type fruit with golden, nutty-flavored flesh. Its space-saving growth habit made it notable among winter squash of its time, since most acorn squash varieties before it required significantly more sprawling room.

common_name: Table Gold Acorn Squash (Golden Acorn Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, allowing room for the bushy, semi-compact vines.

directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger has passed, and keep plants evenly watered through fruit set for the best flavor. Table Gold was bred by horticulturist Dr. Oved Shifriss, known for his work developing compact bush-type squash, and produces bright golden-yellow acorn-shaped fruit on space-saving vines. The tender flesh has a notably nutty, sweet flavor that distinguishes it from the more common dark-green acorn types.

common_name: Dickinson Pumpkin (Kentucky Field Pumpkin, Libby's Select)
subcategory: 19th-century field pumpkin, primary source of U.S. canned pumpkin

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the last frost, in soil that has warmed and with plenty of room for long sprawling vines.

directions: Direct sow in hills after frost danger has passed, giving vines ample room to sprawl, and let fruit fully mature on the vine until the rind hardens and dulls in color. Traced to early nineteenth-century Kentucky and carried to central Illinois by farmer Elijah Dickinson, this tan, oblong pumpkin is more closely related botanically to butternut squash than to typical jack-o'-lantern types. Libby's acquired rights to the strain in 1929, and the Dickinson pumpkin remains the primary variety grown for canned pumpkin in the United States today, prized for its dense, smooth-textured, deep orange flesh.

common_name: Prizewinner Pumpkin (Prize Winner Giant Pumpkin Hybrid)
subcategory: F1 hybrid giant pumpkin for exhibition growing

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into a heavily amended, sun-drenched bed with room to spare.

directions: Start seeds indoors a few weeks before the last frost to maximize the growing season, then transplant into deeply enriched soil with generous room for the vines to sprawl, thinning each plant down to a single developing fruit for maximum size. This F1 hybrid giant pumpkin was bred for exhibition growers chasing very large fruit, with mature specimens commonly reported in the 100 to 300 pound range under attentive feeding and watering. Its smooth, glossy orange rind and classic rounded pumpkin shape make it as suitable for display as it is for competition.

common_name: Big Moon Pumpkin (Giant Orange Exhibition Pumpkin)
subcategory: open-pollinated giant pumpkin for exhibition and carving

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, then transplant once soil is warm, leaving ample space for sprawling vines.

directions: Get a jump on the season by starting seeds indoors, then transplant into rich, well-drained soil with generous spacing once frost danger has passed, watering deeply and consistently as fruit develops. Big Moon is an open-pollinated giant pumpkin variety, registered in the USDA germplasm collection, capable of producing single fruits weighing up to around 200 pounds under good growing conditions. Its smooth orange rind and classic rounded form have made it a long-standing choice for both giant pumpkin hobbyists and fall carving displays.
